bib.title: Professional Software Developers Don't Vibe, They Control: AI Agent Use for Coding in 2025

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Professional Software Developers Don't Vibe, They Control: AI Agent Use for Coding in 2025", Ruanqianqian (Lisa) Huang, Avery Reyna (equal contribution), Sorin Lerner (Cornell), Haijun Xia, Brian Hempel (UC San Diego). arXiv:2512.14012v2 [cs.SE], stamped 18 Aug 2026. Preprint; no venue printed. Studies run Aug-Oct 2025.

COVERAGE: 15 pages. I read chars 0-68,718 of 98,235 line by line: abstract, methods, results, discussion, related work and conclusion. The remaining ~29.5k chars are references, which I did not read (skimmed only the start). The paper has no appendices; the study materials are on an external link (tinyurl.com/devs-using-agents-2025).

FIT: Weak for note 05. The paper does not study "agents don't test" and has no verification-loop, definition-of-done, eval-first, or generation/evaluation-separation material. It is a human-factors qualitative study of how experienced developers supervise agents. The only relevant material is a few lines on how humans verify output (Table 3). Closest fit is 05 as a "verification the user performs" citation (sharpens, not core). Alternative: 08 maturity, as a human-in-the-loop calibration point ("2025 agents cannot autonomously manage large software"). 04 execution boundaries is the weakest fit. If one section, use 05, "verification the user performs".

CORE CLAIM: Experienced developers do not vibe code. They control agents through planning, small steps and active review, because they care about software quality.

HEADLINE NUMBERS (all self-reported or hand-coded; no agent accuracy was measured)
1. Field observations: n=13 developers with 3+ years of professional experience (median 9). One 45-minute session each on a self-chosen task, plus a 30-minute interview. Tools were mostly Cursor (6) and Claude Code (4). Models were Sonnet 3.5-4.5, GPT-5 and others, as printed in Table 1.
   - Nine of 13 "carefully reviewed every change" (9/13, 69%).
   - Three (P1, P4, P5), all on unfamiliar tasks, did not review code but monitored closely.
   - Verification tactics (Table 3): UI testing, IDE or git diff, debugger, CLI tests.
   - Five tested "more systematically" with agents. P6 had agents generate tests for every change.
   - Testing stayed manual for UI, databases and remote apps.
   - Median 1.8 steps executed per prompt (max 5.0). Plans reached 70+ steps but were never executed more than 6 at once.
2. Survey: n=99 of 249 responses (6% rate) from 4,141 emailed GitHub users active in AI-tool repos. Mean 12.8 years of experience. 97 of 99 were male.
   - Mean suitability 4.7/6, enjoyment 5.1/6, "had to modify agent code" 3.0/5.
   - 67 prioritised quality attributes. Correctness was top (20), then readability (18).
   - 50 drove architecture and design themselves.
3. Task suitability counts (suitable:unsuitable mentions, hand-coded):
   - One-shotting code without modification or verification: 5:23.
   - Writing tests: 19:2.
   - Complex tasks: 3:16.
   - Business logic: 2:15.
   - Following well-defined plans: 28:2.
   - Replacing human decision-making: 0:12.
   - "No respondent indicated that agents are suitable for completely autonomous operation."
4. Eight of 13 observed participants said agents did more than asked (extra files, rewrites, unneeded packages).

ABLATION: None. This is a descriptive qualitative study with no comparison conditions and no outcome measure.

QUOTES
- "Importantly, no respondent indicated that agents are suitable for completely autonomous operation, instead the more common sentiment was that of S83: 'I do everything with *assistance* but never let the agent be completely autonomous—I am always reading the output and steering.'" (p.6)
- "Notably, five Observations participants tested code more systematically when using agents, with P6 having agents generate tests for every change to reinforce test-driven development. However, testing remained manual for UI interactions (P4, P10), databases (P8), and remote applications (P10)." (p.5)
- "Human oversight is still needed because LLMs may be unsuitable for one-shotting code without modification/verification (5:23)" (p.7)
- "automated testing in remote or realistic environments, tedious UI debugging through prompting, and understanding why an agent fails or hangs" (p.8, future work; named pain points)

LIMITS (authors and mine)
- The survey sample was deliberately biased toward AI enthusiasts, so it is weak for sentiment. Only 6% responded.
- Observations were small (n=13), single 45-minute sessions with no longitudinal use or full development cycle.
- Gender skew: 92% and 98% male.
- Hand-coded themes with no inter-rater reliability. Suitability thresholds (2.5:1) were the authors' judgment.
- Mostly self-report. Tool versions are 2025 vintage. The authors concede agents have improved since, possibly shifting suitability and reducing the need for line-by-line review.
- Does not show that control or review improves outcomes. The authors say best practices are unvalidated and productivity is unmeasured.
- Cites Becker et al.: a 19% slowdown for experienced open-source maintainers, who estimated a 20% speedup (n=16, 246 tasks).
- Says nothing on verification-loop design, definition of done, or separating generator from evaluator. Test-generation claims are anecdotal (P6).

BUILDS ON
- Karpathy (vibe coding, 2025, as cited [28]).
- Becker et al. [4] (RCT, 2025).
- Kumar et al. [29], Kam et al. [26], Chou et al. [10], Sarkar and Drosos [43] (qualitative studies of agent and vibe-coding use).
- Braun and Clarke-style thematic analysis ([5]).
- Anthropic best-practices guidance [9].
- Reference years are as printed; I did not check the reference list.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Table 3 on p.5 (a table, not a figure). It gives per-participant verification method, diff review and step counts. It is the only part usable for note 05. Fig. 2 (p.5), the annotated P3 prompt with "do just step 1", suits note 03 or prompting, not 05.

PROBLEMS: None in extraction (text clean; tables flattened but readable). No embedded instructions found. Source file: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/03-harness-engineering/sources/huang-2025-professional-software-developers-don-t.pdf
